extracted.intended_audience: naval officers, coastal surveyors, mariners and naturalists conducting coastal exploration
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for coastal surveying, anchorage selection, and natural-history observation while exploring coral islands, reefs, and nearby mainland coasts. Emphasises visual navigation, soundings, landmark bearings, and natural signs (fauna, guano, vegetation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gage Roads anchorage selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the proper berth in Gage Roads: "which is in seven or eight fathoms, on sandy mud, about a mile from the gaol, bearing East by North."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor in 7–8 fathoms on sandy mud about a mile from the gaol (E by N). Avoid anchoring a quarter-mile nearer shore where the bottom shoals rapidly to 4 and 3 fathoms on rocky ground; vessels too near shore are liable to be driven ashore if a breeze comes on while discharging cargo. Many wrecks result from selecting an improper berth to be near shore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify reported shoals by soundings (do not rely solely on charts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported features (e.g., the Turtle Dove shoal) should be checked by actual soundings; charts and prior reports may be in error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: repeated passes and soundings near the assigned position of the Turtle Dove showed no indication of a shoal, suggesting the charted shoal did not exist. Use multiple observations and depth readings from different vessels/boats before trusting reported reefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach coral harbours by eye and exercise utmost vigilance
rubrics_metrics.description: Coral harbours "require to be taken by eye, being full of coral knolls, which necessitate the utmost vigilance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Navigate coral harbours visually rather than relying purely on charts; expect numerous coral knolls and irregular bottom; proceed slowly, keep a good lookout, and be ready to alter course as submarine hazards are sighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use masthead and visual indicators to identify shoals, channels, and limits of danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual signs from a height are essential: "I could clearly distinguish the limit of the danger... The surface of the lagoon was diversified by blue and grey patches, showing the alternations of shoal and deep water; near the centre there appeared to be a channel."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From masthead or other vantage, look for white breakers (limit of danger), blue/grey patches (depth changes), lines of discoloured water, and 'submarine forests' visible in pellucid water to trace channels and safe passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probe suspicious spots with boat soundings before entering or anchoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Before hauling into a bay or anchoring, examine suspicious spots with boat soundings: "we did not haul into the bay until some suspicious spots had been sounded over by a boat."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Send boats ahead to take immediate soundings where the bottom or water colour looks uncertain. Do not commit the ship to an anchorage until shallow spots and coral patches have been checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use leading marks and bearings of prominent landmarks to guide approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Navigate into harbours and through passes by aligning prominent features and following bearings (examples given: Mount Fairfax, Point Moore, sandhills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry lines: use the bearing of recognizable hills, sandhills, or named points to lead into channels (e.g., Mount Fairfax, Point Moore, bare-topped brown sandhill as referenced for Champion Bay; specific bearing alignments given for Recruit Harbour). Record and follow these bearings to steer clear of reefs and spits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer anchoring on sandy mud or fine white sand; avoid rocky shoal ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchorage bottoms of sandy mud or fine white sand are preferable for holding; rocky ground near shore is hazardous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example depths given where good holding occurs: inside bays 5–6 fathoms on fine white sand; Champion Bay anchorage in four fathoms with sheltered aspect. Avoid shallow rocky bottoms (4–3 fathoms) which increase risk of dragging and damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chart depths and currents: use soundings to map channels and outer-reef edges; note current directions and speeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent soundings reveal banks, channels, and the steepness of banks; currents are often measurable and related to wind shifts (examples: current setting NNW a mile an hour; outside reefs no bottom with 250 fathoms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take systematic depth readings across channels (examples: 22–26 fathoms in Geelvink Channel; sudden deepening to no bottom with 250 fathoms indicates steep outer edges). Record current directions and rates, and observe how wind veering changes current settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety procedures for gales and water-spouts: monitor instruments but remain prepared
rubrics_metrics.description: Barometer readings may not always warn of gales; observe changing wind patterns and postpone operations if hazardous phenomena appear ("small water-spouts formed near the ship... induced us to wait until they passed").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep readiness to react (anchors, sails, boats). Do not rush weighing or entering exposed positions when water-spouts or heavy squalls are present. Note the relationship of wind veering to current changes during storms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify guano and assess its economic potential by surface signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Soil layers mixed with guano, seabird burrows, and colony signs indicate valuable guano deposits: "a layer of a kind of soil... in which the seabirds burrow... I believe to contain some of the valuable substance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect low sandy necks and island soils for bird burrows and guano-bearing layers; such islands may merit further enquiry for fertilizer extraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess island water sources cautiously; test for tidal/brackish influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Wells or holes containing water may be brackish and subject to tidal influence: "On the north end of the island was a hole containing brackish water; when we dug it deeper the salt water poured in. The well is on the south point, and the water... rises and falls with the tide."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume surface water is fresh. Dig deeper to test salinity and tidal influence. Be aware that prior human activity (e.g., rows of bottles placed to collect water) may indicate attempts to secure scarce freshwater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize coral reef vertical structure and coral types when examining formations
rubrics_metrics.description: Coral walls and reef composition are vertically zoned: "The reef... is nearly dry at low-water; a portion does not rise so high, projecting out so as to form a narrow shelf, from the edge of which a wall descends almost sheer to the depth of 54 feet. The upper 20 feet are formed of a peculiar kind of coral, growing in the shape of huge fans... The coral forming the lower 34 feet of the wall is of the common large branch kind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying reefs, note the visible coral morphologies (fan-shaped upper growth, large-branch lower growth, brain-stones) and the sheer drop-offs; these features inform judgments about reef formation, depths, and the danger to vessels.
